meta.title: Who really said "It's not the people who vote that count, it's the people who count the votes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Stalin never wrote this pun. The closest is a 1923 remark recalled by his ex-secretary Bazhanov; the idea dates to an 1871 Thomas Nast cartoon.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's not the people who vote that count, it's the people who count the votes'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Stalin's words. A secretary's memoir recalls a 1923 remark about counting party votes; the saying itself goes back to an 1871 Nast cartoon.

answer.label: Not Joseph Stalin — an older saying, reworded
answer.sourceLine: The punning wording appears in no work by Stalin. The idea’s earliest known form is a caption Thomas Nast put in Boss Tweed’s mouth in Harper’s Weekly in October 1871: “As long as I count the Votes, what are you going to do about it?” (Quote Investigator ↗). Stalin’s only link is a 1923 remark about counting votes inside the party, reported later in Boris Bazhanov’s memoirs.

source.heading: The closest documented source

docMeta.dd: Boris Bazhanov, Vospominaniya byvshego sekretarya Stalina (Memoirs of Stalin’s Former Secretary)
1923, recalled by Bazhanov; about winning a majority inside the Communist Party, not public elections

source.excerpt: “Do you know, comrades, what I think about this: I consider it completely unimportant who in the party will vote, or how; but what is extraordinarily important is this—who will count the votes, and how.”
trail: 1871: Thomas Nast’s Harper’s Weekly cartoon “That’s What’s the Matter” has Boss Tweed say, “As long as I count the Votes, what are you going to do about it? say?” This is the earliest match known to Quote Investigator ↗, which credits Nast rather than Tweed.

1923 (as recalled): In his memoirs Boris Bazhanov has Stalin tell Kamenev and Zinoviev that what matters is “who will count the votes, and how.” The next day, he writes, party vote reports printed in Pravda were being falsified (Russian text ↗). Wikiquote ↗ lists the remark under “Contemporary witnesses”, not under Stalin’s own speeches and writings.

2000: “It’s not the people who vote that count. It’s the people who count the votes” went viral during the Bush–Gore recount, with no published source cited (Snopes ↗, rating: Mixture). Slate ↗’s answer at the time: “Almost certainly, no.”
2022: Stalin specialists told PolitiFact ↗ the quote is apocryphal. J. Arch Getty found nothing like it in Stalin’s personal archive, and Mark Kramer said Bazhanov’s account cannot be confirmed.
source.excerptNote: Russian original: «я считаю, что совершенно неважно, кто и как будет в партии голосовать; но вот что чрезвычайно важно, это — кто и как будет считать голоса». The opening clause (“Do you know, comrades…”) is our own rendering of the Russian. The rest follows the English printed in Lend Me Your Ears and on Wikiquote. In Bazhanov’s account Stalin is answering Kamenev’s question about how to win a majority in the party. The popular line “It’s not the people who vote that count…” is a later, looser rewording.

source.rightsNote: The popular wording is an anonymous rewording with no identifiable source, so we assert no copyright status for it. The nearest documented passage is in Bazhanov’s Russian memoir (text © 1980, Tret’ya Volna, Paris). That book and its English translations should be treated as in copyright, so the excerpt above is quoted briefly for commentary.

author.name: Thomas Nast
author.heading: About Thomas Nast
author.bio: Thomas Nast is often called the “Father of the American Cartoon”. His Harper’s Weekly cartoons attacked the Tammany Hall machine of William Marcy “Boss” Tweed. Quote Investigator credits Nast with the 1871 caption “As long as I count the Votes, what are you going to do about it? say?”, the earliest known version of the vote-counting saying. QI thinks Tweed probably never said it himself.

Nearest Stalin-linked text: Boris Bazhanov, Vospominaniya byvshego sekretarya Stalina (St. Petersburg: Vsemirnoe slovo, 1992), chap. 5.

copyAttribution: “It’s not the people who vote that count, it’s the people who count the votes.” — Popularly attributed to Joseph Stalin, but found in none of his works. Closest: a 1923 remark about counting party votes, recalled in Boris Bazhanov’s memoirs. Earliest known form of the idea: Thomas Nast cartoon, Harper’s Weekly, 7 October 1871.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it doesn’t stick
misattribution.intro: The vote-counting quip has drifted between strongmen for more than a century. Stalin is just its latest and most famous host.

items.why: No speech or writing by Stalin contains it. The only link is Bazhanov’s recollection of a 1923 remark about counting votes inside the party. Quote Investigator ↗ says the long gap between the remark and its report lowers its credibility. Historians quoted by PolitiFact ↗ call the Stalin quote apocryphal.

items.scope: “As long as I count the Votes…”
items.why: The words come from Thomas Nast’s satirical 1871 cartoon, not from Tweed. QI ↗ thinks Tweed probably never said it and credits Nast.

items.scope: “I care not who casts the votes…”
items.why: In 1880 The New York Times linked the line to Napoleon while saying that he “failed to remark” it, as reprinted by QI ↗.
An 1877 San Francisco paper credited him. QI ↗ conjectures that this came from political hostility.

items.scope: A similar line, not the source
items.why: His 1972 play Jumpers has “It’s not the voting that’s democracy, it’s the counting.” Snopes ↗ lists it among several earlier non-Stalin versions of the idea.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment goes back to an 1871 Thomas Nast cartoon. The neat “people who vote that count” pun has no known author and was pinned on Stalin long after his death (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it keeps coming back
lead: The line resurfaces whenever an election is contested. Snopes ↗ notes that this exact wording first gained internet notoriety during the 2000 Bush–Gore recount. It came back in 2022 as a meme pairing Stalin with Joe Biden, which PolitiFact ↗ rated False.

Even taken at face value, Bazhanov’s anecdote is narrower than the meme. In the memoir ↗ Stalin is talking about votes in party cell meetings during an internal Bolshevik fight, not public elections. Bazhanov was a hostile witness writing after his defection, and no independent record confirms the remark.
detailsBody: Bazhanov’s preface says he became Stalin’s assistant and secretary of the Politburo on 9 August 1923, fled Soviet Russia on 1 January 1928, and published newspaper articles and a book in France in 1929 and 1930 (Russian text ↗). We have not confirmed whether the vote-counting anecdote was in those early French publications or first appeared in the later Russian memoir.
The 1989 London Observer line “as Stalin is supposed to have said, it’s not who votes that matters but who counts the votes” is the first Stalin attribution in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.
context.pull: “What is extraordinarily important is this — who will count the votes, and how.”
